name: value-object
intent: Model a descriptive concept that has no identity as an immutable object whose equality, hashing and validation are defined by its attributes, so a cluster of attributes that always changes together is created, compared and replaced as one unit.
problem: A cluster of attributes that always changes as a whole is passed around as separate primitives or mutated field by field: validation is duplicated at every call site, partial updates leave inconsistent combinations behind, and equality or lookup by concept (which address, which money amount) has no owner.
context: Domain and application code where a concept is descriptive rather than identified (money, ranges, quantities, addresses, codes), where the same combination of attributes must stay consistent across creation, comparison, hashing and persistence mapping, and where instances are shared across call sites or threads so aliasing bugs and defensive copies have to be eliminated.
benefits: Invariants live with the data: validation and normalisation happen once at construction, so an invalid combination cannot exist afterwards.
Multi-attribute change becomes one concept-level operation: replacing the whole value is atomic and partial updates cannot leave a half-changed cluster.
Equality and hashing by concept work everywhere: value objects are safe set/map keys and compare correctly across serialization round-trips.
No aliasing bugs: an immutable value may be shared, cached and passed between threads without defensive copies, because no holder can mutate it behind another holder's back.
Primitive obsession is removed: typed concepts (Money, EmailAddress, DateRange) give one name and one owner to rules previously scattered over strings and numbers.
Domain behaviour becomes explicit and testable: operations that used to be ad-hoc field fiddling turn into methods that return new values.
Cross-process boundaries become explicit: serialising a value object through APIs, message queues or database columns carries a single semantic unit rather than a tuple of uncoordinated primitives.
tradeoffs: Replace-don't-mutate forces a copy or allocation per change; in hot loops or with large attribute sets this costs throughput unless persistent structures, interning or selective mutability are used.

Attribute-based equality has to be maintained wherever the language does not synthesise it (C, Go beyond comparable fields, JavaScript, TypeScript): adding a field silently changes equality and hash behaviour, and already-stored keys can become unreachable.

Immutability is shallow unless every referenced object is immutable too; exposing a mutable collection or collaborator through a value object reintroduces exactly the aliasing bug the pattern removes.

Identity-less values do not fit frameworks that key by reference (ORM identity maps, caches, memoization hooks) and need explicit mapping work (embedded/owned columns, converters) at the persistence boundary.
Construction moves to validating factories: every call site must funnel through them, so small values that were previously inline literals now need named constructors and error handling.

Memberwise equality is subtly wrong for some attributes: floating-point NaN and signed zero, derived or cached fields, and attributes that must compare case-insensitively or after normalisation all need custom comparison logic.

Thousands of short-lived value object instances in infrastructure code (e.g., message queue serialization) create GC pressure that can meaningfully slow throughput compared to stack-allocated primitives.
Performance optimization techniques (interning, pooling, source generation) add complexity that must be weighed against the actual performance profile of the domain.
ORM integration may require owned/embedded type configuration that varies across frameworks and versions, creating a maintenance surface outside the domain layer.

participants.responsibility: Immutable type that represents the concept as a whole and whose equality and hash are derived from its attributes rather than from identity.
The state that defines the conceptual whole; only attributes that change together and participate in equality belong to the value.
Validates and normalises raw input and hands out only fully constructed values, usually through intention-revealing static factory methods.
Treats equal instances as interchangeable: compares by value, uses values as keys, and replaces instead of mutating.
Holds the value as part of its own state and persists it with (or inside) its own record, since the value has no identity or lifecycle of its own.

use_cases: Money and quantities: amounts with currency or unit, rounding rules and unit-compatible arithmetic.
Validated identifiers and codes: email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs, tax ids or product codes with checksums.
Ranges and periods: date ranges, intervals and validity periods with their own containment, overlap and open-end semantics.
Geographic and postal values: coordinates, locations and addresses carried inside an Order, Shipment or Customer aggregate.
Measurements, rates and percentages in pricing, tariffs and rules that travel through several layers without drifting.
Composite keys for caches, dictionaries and deduplication (tenant + code + version) where equality by state is required.
Validated primitives for domain-specific strings: PersonName, PhoneNumber, Url, CountryCode that carry validation logic.
Complex numbers, vectors, matrices and geometric shapes in computational domains.
Temporal values beyond dates: TimeSlot, HolidaySchedule, BusinessHours with their own scheduling logic.
Financial instruments: exchange rates, interest rates, percentages and ratios with conversion rules.
Discriminated-union variants: modelling mutually exclusive states (open-ended intervals, recurring anniversaries, jurisdictional rules) where a single attribute determines which sub-type applies.
Composite identifiers across storage systems: a storage key combining partition, namespace and version that must be compared and serialised as one unit.
Audit/telemetry metadata: a timestamp plus user plus action cluster that always travels together and is replaced atomically.
Color values: RGB/HSL components with gamut validation and conversion methods.

Rust structs with #[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]: the language generates structural equality over all fields and a field-combining hash, which is what makes the value usable as a HashMap key; Eq is a marker trait that cannot be derived when a field is f64 (NaN breaks reflexivity), so float-carrying values stay only partially comparable.

Python @dataclass(frozen=True): the standard library generates __eq__ over the fields and, only when frozen is also true, a matching __hash__ — the documented recipe for read-only value objects with attribute equality (e.g., a frozen GeoPoint or Temperature passed around without defensive copies).

Java records (JEP 395): java.lang.Record carriers whose compiler-generated equals/hashCode are derived from exactly the record components — the mainstream Java vehicle for identity-less values such as Coordinates, DateRange or Money (amount + currency).
avoid_when: The concept has a lifecycle or must be tracked over time (customer, order, contract): that is an Entity with an identity field, and its equality must not be attribute-based.
It is a thin data carrier whose only job is to cross a boundary and which carries no invariants: a DTO or record with plain fields is simpler.
The concern is a single primitive with no rules: use the primitive; wrap it only where type safety or validation actually earns a Newtype.
The value is huge or expensive to copy (image, document blob, large tree): share it behind a reference with copy-on-write, or store it serialized instead of deep-copying it everywhere.
A framework requires reference identity for its own bookkeeping (identity map, reference-keyed cache, entity tracker): keep that type an entity and expose the value parts as embedded values.

The concept's identity is derived from a composite of attributes in one context but from a stable surrogate ID in another: model it as an Entity in the context that requires tracking and a Value Object where identity is structural.
anti_patterns: A type that carries an identity field (surrogate id, database key) and calls itself a value object: two equal concepts compare unequal, so set/map lookups and duplicate detection fail.
Shallow immutability: the wrapper is frozen or final while the collections or collaborators it exposes stay mutable, so holders of 'the same value' observe each other's changes.
Mutable value instances used as dictionary or set keys: the hash changes after insertion and entries become unreachable.
Equality computed over every field including caches, timestamps and derived state, so logically equal values compare unequal.
Implementing equals/hash by serialising the whole object to a string or JSON on every comparison: correct only by accident, slow, and unstable across key order or formatting.

Reflection-based equality base class that makes it silently impossible to tell which fields participate in equality: adding a new field does not force a hashCode update, so dictionaries silently lose entries.
ValueObjectObsession: wrapping every primitive everywhere in infrastructure code where millions of short-lived objects are created, causing measurable GC pressure without domain modelling benefit.

Making a value object nullable instead of making its fields nullable or using an empty/static instance (e.g., EmptyEmailAddress): spreads null checks throughout the codebase instead of containing them.
Bypassing validation factories: using public constructors or property setters directly so invariants are never enforced and invalid instances can exist.

Storing a value object in a separate database table with its own surrogate key: violates lifetime-shortening (value objects cannot exist without an owner) and reintroduces the identity the pattern removes.

Lombok @Data on JPA entities: @Data generates equals/hashCode from all fields including auto-generated IDs, so an entity inserted into a HashSet before persistence becomes unfindable after the ID is assigned.
design_principles: Encapsulation: invariants are enforced where the state lives, not at each call site.
Immutability and substitutability: equal values are interchangeable, so sharing is safe and defensive copies are unnecessary.
Value semantics: equality and identity are separate concerns; this type chooses equality by state and gives up identity.
High cohesion: exactly the attributes that change together are grouped together.
Problem-domain naming: the type names a domain concept instead of exposing a primitive.
Fail fast: validate and normalise at construction so invalid states are impossible to represent.
Single responsibility within the value: operations that belong to the concept (add, subtract, contains, overlaps) live on the value object, not scattered in client code.
Lifetime shortening: value objects exist only as part of an owning entity or aggregate; they must not be independently persisted, queried or referenced by identity.
best_practices: Validate and normalise in the constructor or a named static factory so an invalid value can never be constructed; make the raw constructor private where the language allows it.
Base equality and hashing only on the attributes of the conceptual whole, and keep them consistent; exclude caches, timestamps and derived values.
Use immutable collections or deep copies for collection attributes, and never return internal mutable state.
Offer copy/with-style transformations (or static combinators) instead of setters; replace the value, do not change it.
Replace primitives with value objects only where validation or behaviour earns it; otherwise the wrapper only adds indirection.
Give the type deterministic, round-trippable serialization when it crosses a boundary, and map it into the owner's record (embedded value/owned type) for persistence.
Prefer ValueObject<T?> over Nullable<ValueObject> when the null or empty state is semantically meaningful to the domain (e.g., an EmptyEmailAddress that is a valid EmailAddress with no value).
Use interning or a static factory cache for frequently used values (e.g., Money.Zero, empty strings) to reduce allocations without sacrificing immutability.
Keep value objects small (typically 1–7 fields); if a value object grows beyond 7 fields, consider whether it is actually an entity or should be decomposed.

For ORM persistence, prefer complex types over owned entities where the framework supports them (EF Core ComplexProperty in EF Core 8+): they have value semantics by default, avoid reference equality surprises, and support ExecuteUpdate.
Avoid reflection-based equality base classes; prefer language features (records, data classes) or explicit GetHashCode/Equals implementations so equality participation is visible and auditable.
Document which attributes participate in equality: add a comment or named method like GetEqualityComponents() that makes the contract explicit.
Test value object equality thoroughly: same values must be equal, different values must be unequal, hash codes must be consistent, and NaN/float edge cases must be handled.
When using value objects as dictionary keys or in HashSets, verify that the type's hash code and equality are deterministic across serialization round-trips (e.g., after JSON deserialization).
Implement operator overloads (+, -, *, /) for numeric value objects (Money, Quantity) so domain code reads naturally; ensure operators return new instances and never mutate.
Seal value object classes to prevent subclassing that can silently break equality symmetry: if a subclass overrides equals without calling super.equals, symmetry or transitivity fails.
Provide both a throwing factory (Create) and a non-throwing alternative (TryCreate, Result<T>) to give callers a path that avoids exceptions for expected validation failures.
For collection-valued value objects, use a frozen or copy-on-read collection type so that callers cannot mutate the internal state through iteration.

When crossing a process boundary (API, message queue), implement the serialisation interface explicitly and route deserialisation through the validating factory to prevent invalid instances from being reconstituted.
Apply the same normalisation in equality as in construction (e.g., lowercase, trim); failing to do so causes logically equal values to compare unequal.
pitfalls: Shallow immutability: freezing the wrapper but exposing mutable collections through getters. The fix is to deep-copy or return immutable wrappers of any collection attribute.

Reflection-based equality base class: using a generic base that auto-generates equality via reflection hides which fields participate, so adding a non-equality field silently breaks hash-based collections. Prefer explicit implementation or language features.

Identity leakage: giving a value object an Id property for ORM convenience defeats its identity-less nature. Use complex types (EF Core) or owned entity types with OwnsOne, not a separate table with a primary key.

Floating-point equality: IEEE 754 floating-point NaN != NaN and +0.0 != -0.0, which breaks the equals-contract requirement that equal objects have equal hash codes. Normalise floats at construction or use integer-based representations (cents instead of fractional dollars).

Case sensitivity drift: constructing a value with lowercase normalisation but comparing with case-sensitive equality causes logically equal values to compare unequal. Apply the same normalisation in equality as in construction.

GC pressure in hot paths: millions of short-lived value object instances in infrastructure code (queues, event streams) create garbage collector pressure. Use value objects primarily in the domain layer; consider primitives in infrastructure.

Nullable vs empty confusion: treating Nullable<ValueObject> as a replacement for proper null handling spreads null checks throughout code. Prefer ValueObject<T?> with an empty/sentinel instance where semantically meaningful.

Serialization round-trip breaks: value objects that use mutable state for caching or lazy evaluation produce different hash codes after deserialization, breaking dictionary lookups. Keep value objects idempotent across serialization.

Cross-type equality: implementing equality between a value object and a primitive or different type that accidentally works (e.g., comparing wrapped string to raw string) creates subtle bugs. Use type-safe comparison only.

ORM LINQ equality on owned entities: EF Core owned entities use reference (identity) equality in LINQ, not attribute equality. Use ComplexProperty (EF Core 8+) instead, which has true value semantics.

Builder bypasses validation: using a builder to construct a value object may skip constructor validation if the build step does not re-validate. Ensure builders call the same validation as constructors.

Performance regression from validation: running full validation (regex, database lookups) on every factory call in hot paths adds measurable latency. Consider separating fast local validation from expensive validation (network, database) where performance matters.

ORM lazy-loaded proxy classes: JPA/Hibernate proxies subclass your value object so getClass() != the actual type, breaking instanceof and symmetric equality. Use getClass() equality check or unwrap the proxy before comparison.

Lombok @Data on JPA entities: @Data generates equals/hashCode from all persistent fields including auto-generated IDs, so an entity inserted into a HashSet before persistence becomes unfindable after the ID is assigned. Use @EqualsAndHashCode(onlyExplicitlyIncluded) with explicit ID inclusion.

JSON deserialisation bypassing constructor: frameworks like encoding/json in Go or System.Text.Json in .NET write directly to fields via reflection, bypassing validation logic in the constructor. Implement custom deserialisers or use constructor-binding features.

Flyweight confusion: shared immutable value objects (e.g., a shared Currency instance) must be truly immutable; if a client casts away const or uses reflection to mutate state, all holders observe the mutation.

Partial equality fields: shipping address equality on street/city/postal/country but ignoring delivery-instructions is correct, but must be documented; a developer who adds a field without understanding the equality model will break dedup logic silently.

Wrong move: declaring a Java record component as an array or mutable List because records are 'immutable' -> the array is compared by reference, so two records with identical contents compare unequal, and callers who keep the original array can mutate the value after construction -> instead defensively copy in the compact constructor and accessor, override equals/hashCode with Arrays.equals/Arrays.hashCode, or hold an immutable List.of/List.copyOf.

Wrong move: marking a Python value object @dataclass without frozen=True because you only wanted generated __eq__ -> the dataclass sets __hash__ to None (PEP 557: eq without frozen means unhashable), so using an instance as a dict key or set member raises TypeError -> instead set frozen=True (eq=True is the default), which generates a consistent __hash__, and use dataclasses.replace(...) instead of mutation.

Wrong move: putting a float-based measurement (e.g., Celsius with an f64 field) straight into a HashMap because the struct derives PartialEq + Hash -> derived Eq is rejected for float fields since IEEE 754 NaN violates reflexivity, and silently switching to a bit-cast hash makes NaN or -0.0 keys unreachable -> instead normalise to an integer representation (milli-degrees, cents) or wrap the float in a newtype with total-order equality and a normalising Hash.

related_patterns_notes.entity: The primary complement: entities have identity-based equality, value objects have attribute-based equality. Entities own value objects; value objects can never own entities.
related_patterns_notes.immutable-object: Value objects are inherently immutable; this pattern provides the structural pattern while immutability is the enforced state property.
related_patterns_notes.embedded-value: A persistence-specific expression of value objects: stored inline within the owning record rather than as a separate table with foreign key.
related_patterns_notes.newtype: A simple single-attribute value object wrapper around a primitive that provides type safety and validation without multi-attribute semantics.
related_patterns_notes.money: A specialized value object for currency amounts with arithmetic operations, rounding rules and currency compatibility checks.
related_patterns_notes.quantity: A specialized value object for measurement values with units, enabling unit-safe arithmetic and conversion.
related_patterns_notes.type-safe-enum: Value objects can be used to model enumerated concepts with associated data, extending the safety of enums to more complex states.
related_patterns_notes.null-object: A value object representing an absence of value (e.g., EmptyEmailAddress) that differs from null references, reducing null checks throughout the codebase. Prefer ValueObject<T?> over Nullable<ValueObject> where the null/empty state is meaningful to the domain concept.
related_patterns_notes.state-pattern: While both model behaviour that varies with state, the State Pattern uses distinct objects with identity (which state am I in?), whereas value objects are interchangeable by attribute equality and do not track transitions.
related_patterns_notes.builder: Builders can construct value objects with many optional fields while still enforcing invariants at the final build step, especially useful when the VO has 4+ fields or complex cross-field validation.
related_patterns_notes.specification: Specs can encapsulate validation rules that value object factories delegate to, keeping validation logic reusable and composable beyond construction.
related_patterns_notes.composite: Composite patterns combine simple objects into trees; value objects are often the leaf nodes in a composite design (e.g., LineItem containing Money values) and must not carry identity that would conflict with composite equality rules.
related_patterns_notes.flyweight: Immutable value objects with a small domain (e.g., Currency, CountryCode) are natural Flyweight instances: one shared object per unique value eliminates redundant allocation when the same value appears across thousands of entities.
related_patterns_notes.cqrs: In CQRS read models, value objects are the natural vocabulary: a read projection returns immutable DTOs composed of value objects that describe what was read, without identity or behaviour, matching the query side's needs precisely.
related_patterns_notes.result: Factory methods on value objects return Result<T, E> (or Either) rather than throwing, making validation failures explicit in the caller's type and preventing exceptions for expected validation scenarios in business-critical construction paths.
